parsed_answer.content: Designing for exactly-once semantics and determining whether it is truly possible end-to-end represents one of the most intellectually rigorous challenges in distributed systems engineering. To unpack this, we must deconstruct the core concepts: exactly-once semantics (EOS), the theoretical boundaries of distributed consensus, and end-to-end pipelines. Exactly-once semantics guarantee that every record produced, transmitted, and processed results in a single, observable state change within the target system, even in the presence of node failures, network partitions, or duplicate message deliveries. In practice, pure end-to-end exactly-once processing is an engineering illusion. The Fallacies of Distributed Computing—specifically the unreliability of networks and independent system failures—dictate that message transport layers can only guarantee at-least-once delivery (retrying until an acknowledgment is received) or at-most-once delivery (fire and forget). Therefore, true end-to-end EOS is not a property of a single messaging broker; rather, it is an architectural illusion achieved through idempotent processing and transactional boundaries spanning the data producer, the streaming engine (such as Apache Kafka or Apache Flink), and the downstream datastore.

items: At the transport layer, streaming engines like Kafka achieve 'exactly-once' processing by coupling idempotent producers (using sequence numbers and producer IDs) with transactional coordinators that write both the consumed offsets and output states atomically to a transaction log.

Downstream persistence breaks the illusion if the target database lacks native support for conditional writes, upserts, or distributed two-phase commit (2PC) protocols, forcing reliance on business-level idempotency keys.

Stateful stream processors like Flink utilize the Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshot algorithm (asynchronous barrier snapshotting) to checkpoint operator states alongside input stream offsets, enabling deterministic recovery to a precise logical time.

parsed_answer.content: Senior architectural warning: Never trust framework marketing claims of 'end-to-end exactly-once.' While stream processors can guarantee exactly-once processing *within their own internal state boundaries*, the moment a side effect occurs—such as calling an external third-party payment gateway API, sending an email, or writing to a non-transactional datastore—the guarantee is immediately broken. True EOS requires that every external interaction be inherently idempotent or wrapped in an outbox pattern with compensation logic.

title: How do you design for exactly-once semantics? Is exactly-once really possible end to end?
